# Somadattajātaka (Ja 211)

**ID:** Ja 211
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Somadattajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Somadattajātaka* (Ja 211), titled in English *The Farmer’s Son Somadatta*, is a canonical Pali birth-story preserved in the Jātaka collection. In the frame narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha delivers the teaching while residing at Jetavana with reference to the Elder Lāḷudāyī (or Laludayi, "the Simpleton"), a monk notorious for his nervous embarrassment and habitual blundering, who invariably uttered the wrong words during formal gatherings [Fausböll 1879; Burlingame 1921a].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta is born as Somadatta, a skilled courtier who has won the favor and affection of the king of Benares [Burlingame 1921a; Burlingame 1921b; Fausböll 1879]. His father, a rustic brahmin named Aggidatta, earns a livelihood by farming with two oxen [Burlingame 1921a; Burlingame 1921b]. When one ox dies, the father asks Somadatta to petition the king for another [Burlingame 1921a; Burlingame 1921b]. Somadatta, unwilling to presume upon royal favor, instructs his slow-witted father to request it himself, spending a year drilling him in a cemetery using bundles of grass to represent the king, viceroy, and commander-in-chief, and teaching him a verse of solicitation [Burlingame 1921a; Burlingame 1921b; Fausböll 1879]. When brought before the king, however, the nervous farmer misspeaks and recites a verse begging the king to take away his remaining ox [Burlingame 1921a; Fausböll 1879]. Amused by the error, the king generously bestows oxen, chariots, and a village upon him [Burlingame 1921a; Fausböll 1879]. The Buddha identifies Lāḷudāyī as the foolish father and himself as Somadatta [Burlingame 1921b; Fausböll 1879]. Bailey and Mabbett cite this tale as sociological testimony regarding impoverished, secularized brahmins who engaged in agriculture and struggled to retain or recite formal verses correctly [Bailey and Mabbett 2003].

This narrative also appears in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* as part of an exposition on Lāḷudāyī's past karma [Burlingame 1921a; Burlingame 1921b]. DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal text reuse with the second volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Atk S0513a2), sharing three matches totaling 315 characters [DharmaNexus]. No cross-language parallels in Chinese, Tibetan, or Sanskrit are recorded [DharmaNexus].
